"title": "A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors",
"authors": "Nishi Kumari, Ayush Upadhyay, Kishan Kalia, Rakesh Kumar, Kanika Tuteja, Rani Paul, Eugenia Covernton, Tina Sharma, Vinod Scaria, Anshu Bhardwaj",
"field_subfield": "Computational chemistry / cheminformatics applied to antiviral drug discovery",
"type_of_paper": "Dataset/knowledgebase resource with systematic evaluation and prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors",
"executive_summary": "Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly lethal henipavirus (genus Henipavirus, family Paramyxoviridae) causing severe disease with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%, and it is listed by the WHO 'R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases' (2018) as requiring accelerated research and development. Despite outbreaks in Malaysia, Bangladesh, India, and elsewhere, no drug is under clinical trial, and existing antivirals such as ribavirin, favipiravir (T-705), and remdesivir have shown limited or experimental efficacy. The authors developed the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK), a web-based platform built on open-source LAMP technology, to systematically curate, evaluate, and prioritize NiV inhibitors. Data were collected from PubMed and Google using the query 'Nipah', yielding 838 papers initially considered, which were scored (10, 5, 4, or 0) and manually curated. A separate team independently re-performed curation to ensure data quality, with errors marked in red and verified entries marked green. The final knowledgebase contains 182 entries, of which 125 are small molecule inhibitors and 98 are unique NiV inhibitors with available structures. IC50/EC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM across 182 entries and 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM for the 125 small molecule entries. More than 1800 (1875) descriptors were computed using PaDel software, and clustering was performed using NNeib (version 5.12.0) and Jarp (version 6.0.2) with a dissimilarity threshold of 0.15. The physicochemical properties were compared with FDA approved compounds (2346) and antivirals from the Enamine library (4644). Using DruLito filters, only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than the CMC filter. A combined evidence approach prioritized 11 NVIs based on assay robustness, with NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passing 6 DruLito filters and being accepted in FAF drugs analysis. The platform supports simple search, query builder, and structure search (SMILES, SDF, MOL, and JSME drawing), and allows community submission of new inhibitors. The study emphasizes that prioritization was based not only on druglike properties but also on the robustness of the assays used to identify the compounds. The knowledgebase is publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah, and the physicochemical browsing interface is at http://bioinfo.imtech.res.in/anshu/nipah/. The authors highlight the chemical diversity of the library, noting that clustering resulted in 90 clusters, of which 84 (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons and 14 (15.5% of NVIs) were non-singletons. This diversity suggests multiple structural scaffolds and pharmacophore features that could be exploited for drug development. The platform is designed to be continuously enhanced through community contributions, reflecting the authors' belief that engaging the wider scientific community is essential for the future of drug discovery for outbreak strains. The study provides a centralized resource for the community to submit and access NVIs in a seamless manner, and the authors note that these compounds may be utilized for their antiviral activity against other viruses as well. Overall, the paper presents a well-curated, publicly accessible knowledgebase that combines multiple lines of evidence to prioritize druglike, non-toxic NiV inhibitors for further development.",

summary.title: A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors
summary.authors: Nishi Kumari, Ayush Upadhyay, Kishan Kalia, Rakesh Kumar, Kanika Tuteja, Rani Paul, Eugenia Covernton, Tina Sharma, Vinod Scaria, Anshu Bhardwaj
summary.field_subfield: Computational chemistry / cheminformatics applied to antiviral drug discovery
summary.type_of_paper: Dataset/knowledgebase resource with systematic evaluation and prioritization of Nipah virus inhibitors
summary.executive_summary: Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly lethal henipavirus (genus Henipavirus, family Paramyxoviridae) causing severe disease with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%, and it is listed by the WHO 'R&D Blueprint list of priority diseases' (2018) as requiring accelerated research and development. Despite outbreaks in Malaysia, Bangladesh, India, and elsewhere, no drug is under clinical trial, and existing antivirals such as ribavirin, favipiravir (T-705), and remdesivir have shown limited or experimental efficacy. The authors developed the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK), a web-based platform built on open-source LAMP technology, to systematically curate, evaluate, and prioritize NiV inhibitors. Data were collected from PubMed and Google using the query 'Nipah', yielding 838 papers initially considered, which were scored (10, 5, 4, or 0) and manually curated. A separate team independently re-performed curation to ensure data quality, with errors marked in red and verified entries marked green. The final knowledgebase contains 182 entries, of which 125 are small molecule inhibitors and 98 are unique NiV inhibitors with available structures. IC50/EC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM across 182 entries and 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM for the 125 small molecule entries. More than 1800 (1875) descriptors were computed using PaDel software, and clustering was performed using NNeib (version 5.12.0) and Jarp (version 6.0.2) with a dissimilarity threshold of 0.15. The physicochemical properties were compared with FDA approved compounds (2346) and antivirals from the Enamine library (4644). Using DruLito filters, only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than the CMC filter. A combined evidence approach prioritized 11 NVIs based on assay robustness, with NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passing 6 DruLito filters and being accepted in FAF drugs analysis. The platform supports simple search, query builder, and structure search (SMILES, SDF, MOL, and JSME drawing), and allows community submission of new inhibitors. The study emphasizes that prioritization was based not only on druglike properties but also on the robustness of the assays used to identify the compounds. The knowledgebase is publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah, and the physicochemical browsing interface is at http://bioinfo.imtech.res.in/anshu/nipah/. The authors highlight the chemical diversity of the library, noting that clustering resulted in 90 clusters, of which 84 (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons and 14 (15.5% of NVIs) were non-singletons. This diversity suggests multiple structural scaffolds and pharmacophore features that could be exploited for drug development. The platform is designed to be continuously enhanced through community contributions, reflecting the authors' belief that engaging the wider scientific community is essential for the future of drug discovery for outbreak strains. The study provides a centralized resource for the community to submit and access NVIs in a seamless manner, and the authors note that these compounds may be utilized for their antiviral activity against other viruses as well. Overall, the paper presents a well-curated, publicly accessible knowledgebase that combines multiple lines of evidence to prioritize druglike, non-toxic NiV inhibitors for further development.

Research Context
Nipah virus is a highly lethal pathogen with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%. NiV is listed by the WHO as a priority disease requiring accelerated R&D. No drug is currently under clinical trial against Nipah virus. Existing antivirals have shown limited or contradictory efficacy. No systematic evaluation of reported NiV inhibitors has been performed. Existing antiviral databases lack Nipah-specific focus. Reported NiV inhibitors are scattered datasets with limited evaluation. The need is for a centralized resource to systematically evaluate NiV inhibitors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to systematically evaluate and prioritize NiV inhibitors. The study aims to create a well-curated knowledgebase of NiV inhibitors. The hypothesis is that a combined evidence approach can prioritize druglike, non-toxic compounds. The hypothesis is that prioritization should combine druglike properties with assay robustness. The predicted outcome is that some compounds will pass DruLito and PAINS filters. The predicted outcome is that some compounds will be prioritized based on assay robustness. The predicted outcome is that prioritized compounds will resemble FDA approved drugs. The predicted outcome is that the knowledgebase will enable community submission of new inhibitors.

Methodological Details
The main data sources were PubMed and Google. Papers were retrieved using the query 'Nipah'. 838 papers were initially considered for data-mining. Papers were scored using a 10, 5, 4, or 0 system. Papers with scores 10, 5, and 4 were considered for further study. All selected papers were manually curated into the NVIK sheet. A separate team independently re-performed curation for quality. Errors were marked in red and verified entries in green. Each entry was tagged with the contributor's email Id. The knowledgebase is stored in the NVIK-Open resource Sheet. The platform was built using open-source LAMP technology. The platform also used PHP, HTML, JavaScript, AJAX, and CSS. The final knowledgebase contains 182 entries. The focus was on small molecule inhibitors, which were 125 entries. The remaining 57 entries were either peptide or lacked complete information. Of 125 entries, 98 are unique Nipah inhibitors. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 compounds. Structures are available for all 98 inhibitors. More than 1800 descriptors were computed using PaDel software. Near neighbours were identified using NNeib (version 5.12.0). Clusters were obtained using Jarp (version 6.0.2). A dissimilarity threshold of 0.15 was used for clustering. The comparison used FDA approved compounds (2346) and Enamine antivirals (4644). Drug likeness was assessed using DruLito with eight filters. Physicochemical properties were browsed at a dedicated interface. The knowledgebase is publicly available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah. The project began in May 2018.

Procedures And Architectures
The platform provides simple search, query builder, and structure search. Simple Search retrieves information using text-based queries. The query builder enables complex queries with logical operators. Structure search supports SMILES, SDF, and MOL formats. Users can draw compounds in the JSME browser for search. A submission form allows submission of new compounds. The database lists statistics and physicochemical properties. Clustering used a Jarvis-Patrick approach with a 0.15 threshold. CIRCOS was customized to represent physicochemical relationships. In CIRCOS, 98 inhibitors are defined with a band width of 1000. Compound clusters were visualized using Cytoscape. The platform allows browsing by major fields and physicochemical properties. The platform supports submission and assessment of new molecules. The platform enables seamless community access and submission. The platform is designed for continuous community enhancement.

Key Results
The knowledgebase contains 182 entries. 125 entries are small molecule inhibitors. 98 entries are unique Nipah inhibitors. EC50/IC50 values were obtained for 70 compounds. Structures are available for all 98 inhibitors. EC50/IC50 values range from 0.25 nM to 7562710 nM for 182 entries. EC50/IC50 values range from 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM for 125 small molecule entries. 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. Clustering resulted in 90 clusters. 84 clusters (93.3% of NVIs) were singletons. 14 clusters (15.5% of NVIs) were non-singletons. The library is chemically diverse. Comparison used FDA approved compounds (2346) and Enamine antivirals (4644). Most NVIs resemble FDA approved drugs and Enamine compounds. Drugs with good oral availability have TopoPSA ≤ 140 Å2 and rotatable bonds ≤ 10. There are 34 NVIs similar to 76 FDA approved drugs. 5'-deoxy-5'-methylthioadenosine (NVIC0097) is similar to four FDA molecules. DruLito screens compounds based on eight filters. Only two of 91 compounds passed all filters other than the CMC filter. 11 NVIs were prioritized based on assay robustness. NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters. These three compounds were accepted in FAF drugs analysis. NVIC0048 displayed high overlap with all six physicochemical parameter ranges. NVIC0032 exhibits better activity among the three. Prioritized NVIs have physicochemical values closer to FDA approved compounds. The platform allows submission of new inhibitors by the community.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The combined evidence approach prioritizes based on both druglike properties and assay robustness. The chemical diversity suggests multiple scaffolds for drug development. Singletons indicate that most inhibitors are structurally unique. Non-singleton clusters may reveal common pharmacophore features. Similarity to FDA approved drugs supports drug repurposing. Overlap with FDA approved compounds indicates druglike features. Prioritization based on assay robustness adds a new dimension. The platform enables continuous community enhancement. The compounds may be utilized for antiviral activity against other viruses. The knowledgebase provides a centralized resource for the community. The platform supports seamless access and submission. The future of drug discovery for outbreak strains is in community engagement. The study correlates computed properties with experimentally reported bioactivity. The study proposes a list of prioritized candidates. The platform facilitates further analysis and prioritization.
